meta.title: Getting a Reply From Someone Far Above You
meta.subtitle: How to reach the person who never answers strangers
meta.description: A field manual for getting a real reply from someone well above your level — who to target, how to get near them, what to say first, and what to do with the meeting once you get it.
meta.author: AI

cards.title: Don't Aim for the Top Person First
cards.hook: The CEO gets 200 messages a day. Their chief of staff gets 12 — and remembers who sent them. Aim one rung down.
cards.truth:
Top people have zero time and zero reason to answer a stranger.
• The person one rung down has room on their calendar and something to prove.
• They get credit for finding you before their boss does.
• Most people waste their one shot aiming at the name on the door.
cards.remember: Aim one rung down — they have time and something to prove.
cards.theySee: A junior exec they've never heard of, asking something only they personally could answer well.

signals.t: They post publicly that their inbox is out of control.
They changed jobs or got promoted in the last 90 days.
They quote or defend their boss's decisions in public posts.
Their calendar link or bio says they take outside meetings.

steps.title: Map the rung below
steps.desc: List the 3 people who report to the top person and touch your topic.

steps.title: Pick the one with something to prove
steps.desc: Choose whoever is newest, most junior, or most publicly hungry for wins.

steps.title: Check for a fresh win
steps.desc: Search their name plus the last 90 days for a launch, promotion, or talk.

cards.script: "I saw you led the rollout of X — I have a question only someone who ran that would know the answer to."
cards.watchFor: They answer within a day and ask a follow-up question back.
cards.ifItFails: They forward you to their boss's assistant instead of answering. Don't chase the forward — it's a dead end built to make you disappear quietly. Go one rung down from them instead, to the specific person who touched the exact case you're asking about. Send: "Got redirected here — quick one for whoever ran the migration in March."
cards.counter:
If a stranger reaches out to your junior instead of you, they are running this move.
• Notice the message names your junior's specific work, not your title.
• Ask your junior what was actually asked and why.
• Loop in early if the ask is really meant for you — don't let it bypass you.
cards.insight: Everyone fights over the one inbox at the top and ignores the four inboxes one level down. The harder part is picking the right rung — too low and they can't say yes to anything that matters.
cards.when: You want a reply from someone whose name is way above yours on the org chart or industry ladder.
cards.example: Derek wanted the CMO's attention at a Fortune 500 firm. Instead he emailed the newly hired VP of Growth, who had zero inbound and something to prove. She replied in four hours and became his internal champion for the next two years.

cards.title: Find the One Whose Job Is Made Better By You
cards.hook: Nobody replies to be nice. They reply when your message solves a problem sitting on their desk.
cards.truth:
People answer messages that make their own job easier, not messages that make them feel good.
• Find whose metric, launch, or headache your information touches.
• They stop reading you as a stranger and start reading you as a resource.
• Most people pitch their own need first and lose the reader in line one.
cards.remember: Solve their problem — never ask for their pity.
cards.theySee: Someone who clearly did homework on their actual problem, not their title.

signals.t: They posted or spoke about a specific problem in the last month.
Their role or bio ties directly to a number you can move.
You have information, a contact, or data they don't have.
They have a deadline or launch coming where your input matters.

steps.title: List their stated problem
steps.desc: Find one line where they named a challenge, in a post, talk, or interview.

steps.title: Match your value to that line
steps.desc: Write one sentence connecting what you have to that exact problem.

steps.title: Drop the ask from line one
steps.desc: Lead your message with their problem, save your ask for line three.

cards.script: "Saw your note about slow onboarding numbers — I ran the same fix at [Company] and cut it by 40%."
cards.watchFor: They reply asking how you did it, not who you are.
cards.ifItFails: They read it and say 'interesting, thanks' with no next step. That's a polite dead end, not a no — they don't yet see the size of the win. Send one follow-up with a number: "That 40% cut was worth about $200K a year here — happy to walk through it in 10 minutes if useful."
cards.counter:
If someone opens by solving your stated problem, they're running this play on you.
• Notice they quote your own words back before asking for anything.
• Ask what they actually want before you get impressed.
• Test them with one small question and see if they still deliver.
cards.insight: Self-interest beats charity in every inbox, every time. The next problem is timing — the same message sent a month too early or late reads as noise.
cards.when: You're choosing between three possible people to reach out to and don't know who to pick.
cards.example: Priya wanted budget from a VP she'd never met. She skipped the intro and opened with the VP's own stated goal: cutting support costs 20% this year. The VP replied same day asking for her deck.

cards.title: Check What They Post Before You Write Anything
cards.hook: They can tell in one sentence if you did your homework. Most people can't.
cards.truth:
Everyone can smell a copy-paste message inside three words.
• Their public posts tell you what they care about right now.
• A message that quotes their own words back proves you're not spam.
• Most people skip this step and write a message that fits anyone.
cards.remember: Read their last 20 posts before you write one line to them.
cards.theySee: A message that references something they said two weeks ago, not a generic compliment.

signals.t: They wrote or spoke publicly in the last 30 days.
They mention the same topic across three or more posts.
They reply to comments that ask a sharp, specific question.
They've complained publicly about vague or copy-paste outreach.

steps.title: Pull their last 20 public items
steps.desc: Read their last 20 posts, talks, or interviews in one sitting.

steps.title: Circle the repeated theme
steps.desc: Write down the one topic that shows up three or more times.

steps.title: Quote one line back
steps.desc: Use their own phrase or number in your first message, word for word.

cards.script: "You said last month that 'speed beats perfect' on your team — I built something that tests that exact idea."
cards.watchFor: They respond referencing the same post you quoted, confirming they noticed.
cards.ifItFails: You quote them and they still don't answer — meaning the topic wasn't personal enough, just a talking point. Switch to something they said about their own team or a decision they made, not a public opinion. Send: "Different angle — saw you shipped X in Q2. Curious how you picked that over Y."
cards.counter:
If a stranger quotes your own words back at you, check what they actually want.
• Notice the compliment lands right before an ask.
• Ask yourself if the quote is accurate or just flattering.
• Answer the ask on your terms, not the timeline they set.
cards.insight: Homework is the cheapest signal of seriousness there is, and almost nobody does it. The next problem is using what you learn without sounding like you're reciting it.
cards.when: You've picked your target and you're about to write the first message.
cards.example: Tom read six months of a director's tweets before writing one word. He quoted her own line about 'shipping ugly and fast' back to her in his message. She replied: 'Finally someone who actually reads this stuff.'

cards.title: Skip the Person Who Just Got Promoted
cards.hook: The first three months in a new seat, people play safe, not bold. Wrong window to ask for anything.
cards.truth:
New power spends its first months proving it deserves the seat, not handing out favors.
• A fresh promotion means they're watched closely by their own boss.
• Any reply to a stranger feels like a risk they can't afford yet.
• Most people rush the ask right when the target is least free to say yes.
cards.remember: Wait 90 days — a brand-new boss is too scared to risk you.
cards.theySee: A stranger asking for something before they've even found the bathroom on the new floor.

signals.t: Their profile shows a start or promotion date under 90 days old.
Their public posts turned more careful and less personal recently.
They mention 'learning the team' or 'getting up to speed' often.

steps.title: Note the date
steps.desc: Check LinkedIn or a press release for the exact change date.

steps.title: Set a 90-day reminder
steps.desc: Write yourself a note to reach out after day 90, not before.

steps.title: Send something low-stakes now
steps.desc: If you must reach out early, send only a congratulations, no ask.

cards.script: "Congrats on the new role — no ask here, just wanted to say the team's lucky to have you."
cards.watchFor: They reply warmly to the no-ask message, which opens the door for later.
cards.ifItFails: You waited but they're still guarded past 90 days — some new leaders stay defensive for six months or more. Drop the direct ask and route through someone already on their team who can vouch for you first. Send that connector: "Would you be open to a two-line intro when it feels right?"
cards.counter:
If someone congratulates you right after a promotion, notice if it comes with strings.
• A pure congratulations needs no reply — a hidden ask usually gets a fast follow-up.
• Wait to see if a second message arrives within a week.
• If it does, judge the ask on its own, not on the goodwill from message one.
cards.insight: Timing beats wording almost every time in this game. The next question is whether you can remember to wait when you're excited to reach out right now.
cards.when: The person you want to reach just changed roles, got promoted, or joined a new company.
cards.example: Wei wanted a favor from a newly promoted SVP. He held off for three months, sending only a congratulations note in week one. In month four, his real ask got a same-day yes.

cards.title: Find Who Already Has Their Ear
cards.hook: One name attached to yours changes everything. Find who already gets their reply.
cards.truth:
Trust transfers. A message that arrives through someone they already trust skips the filter.
• Every big name has 3-5 people whose messages they always open.
• Getting near one of those people is worth more than a perfect pitch.
• Most people search for the target's email instead of their inner circle.
cards.remember: A warm intro from someone they trust beats your best cold message.
cards.theySee: A name they recognize in the subject line or intro, not a stranger.

signals.t: The same 2-3 names appear tagged in their posts repeatedly.
They appeared on a panel, podcast, or byline with someone.
A mutual contact shares their old school, team, or company.
They reply personally to specific people's comments, not everyone's.

steps.title: List their public tags
steps.desc: Scroll their last 50 posts and note every name they tag or thank.

steps.title: Rank by closeness to you
steps.desc: Sort those names by how close you are to reaching each one.

steps.title: Ask the closest one for a read, not a push
steps.desc: Ask them to look at your message before asking for an intro.

cards.script: "Before I reach out to [Name], would you mind a quick look at this message? Two lines, want to make sure it lands right."
cards.watchFor: The bridge person offers to forward it themselves, unprompted.
cards.ifItFails: The bridge person reads it but won't forward — they don't want to spend their own credibility on you yet. Ask them directly what would need to be true before they'd feel good making the intro, then go build that thing. Say: "Fair. What would make this an easy yes for you to pass along?"
cards.counter:
If someone asks you to 'just take a look' at a message meant for your contact, notice the real ask.
• They want your name attached, not your notes.
• Give feedback only, and say plainly if you won't forward it.
• If you do forward it, say why in one line so your name stays clean.
cards.insight: Borrowed trust is the fastest currency in this game, and it's finite — spend a bridge person's name twice and they stop opening your messages too. The harder part is knowing which bridge is worth burning.
cards.when: You know who you want to reach but have zero direct connection to them.
cards.example: Nora couldn't reach a startup founder directly. She found the founder's old co-founder, who reacted to every one of the founder's posts, and asked him to glance at her message first. He forwarded it himself within a day.

cards.title: Use a Shared Alma Mater or Old Team
cards.hook: People trust their own tribe first. Find the shared past before you write the first line.
cards.truth:
People drop their guard fastest for someone who shares a past marker with them.
• A shared school, team, or city signals you're not a total stranger.
• It buys you three extra seconds of attention before they decide to skip.
• Most people bury this fact in paragraph two instead of leading with it.
cards.remember: Any shared past — school, job, city — opens the door faster.
cards.theySee: Someone from the same world, not a random name in the feed.

signals.t: Their bio lists the same university, program, or year as yours.
They worked at a company you also worked at, even years apart.
Their profile or interviews mention a city or town you're from.

steps.title: Find the exact overlap
steps.desc: Check their bio for school, past jobs, teams, or hometown matches.

steps.title: Name it in the first line
steps.desc: Open with the shared marker before anything else in the message.

steps.title: Keep it short, not sentimental
steps.desc: State the connection in one line, skip the nostalgia paragraph.

cards.script: "Fellow [University] '14 grad here — saw you're now running X, wanted to say congrats and ask a quick question."
cards.watchFor: They reply mentioning the shared place themselves, extending the connection.
cards.ifItFails: They don't respond to the shared-past line — it's a weak tie on its own, not a strong enough hook. Pair it next time with a specific reason tied to their current work, not just the past. Send: "Following up — also saw your team just launched X, and that's exactly the space I'm asking about."
cards.counter:
If a stranger opens with a shared school or old job, notice it's a door-opener, not proof of anything.
• A real connection can be checked in ten seconds — verify it.
• Answer based on the actual ask, not the warm feeling.
• If it doesn't check out, say nothing and let the message die.
cards.insight: Shared past buys attention, not trust — those are different currencies and people confuse them constantly. The next move is turning three seconds of goodwill into something that survives after the flattery wears off.
cards.when: You share a school, past employer, hometown, or old team with your target.
cards.example: Jamal noticed his target went to the same small college fifteen years earlier. He opened his message with the shared school, one line, no story. The reply came back mentioning a professor they'd both had.

cards.title: Comment Where They Already Are, Before You DM
cards.hook: By the time your message lands, you want your name to already look familiar. Get seen first, ask second.
cards.truth:
A name feels safer the second time you see it, even without a reason.
• Sharp comments on their posts plant your name before any ask.
• When your message arrives, it's a familiar name, not a stranger.
• Most people skip this and go straight to the cold DM.
cards.remember: Comment for two weeks before you ever slide into their inbox.
cards.theySee: A commenter who keeps adding something useful, not just 'great post'.

signals.t: You've commented something specific on 3+ of their posts.
They liked or replied to one of your comments already.
Other people in their comment section start replying to you too.

steps.title: Pick 3-4 recent posts
steps.desc: Choose posts from the last month with real content, not filler.

steps.title: Add one sharp comment each
steps.desc: Write a comment that adds a fact, number, or counterpoint, not praise.

steps.title: Wait two weeks, then DM
steps.desc: Send your direct message only after two weeks of visible comments.

cards.script: (Comment, not DM) "Counterpoint on the retention number — we saw the opposite result until we changed X."
cards.watchFor: They like or reply to your comment, or start recognizing your name in the thread.
cards.ifItFails: Two weeks pass and they never react to any comment — you're invisible in a big feed. Switch targets to a smaller, second-degree connection of theirs who does react, and use that person as your bridge instead. Comment there and ask that connector directly for a two-line intro.
cards.counter:
If a name keeps showing up sharp in your comments before a DM lands, notice the setup.
• Check if their comments taught you something or just flattered you.
• Read the eventual DM on its own merit, not on comment history.
• Ask a question that filters real value from a warm-up act.
cards.insight: Familiarity is manufactured, not accidental, and most people manufacture it badly with empty praise. The next problem is content — a comment with nothing in it does zero work no matter how many times you post it.
cards.when: Your target posts regularly and you have weeks before you need a reply.
cards.example: Elena commented sharp, specific counterpoints on a VC's posts for three weeks before ever messaging him. By the time she sent a DM, he already recognized her name and replied within the hour.

cards.title: Get Introduced Instead of Cold Messaging
cards.hook: You can't self-certify. Someone else has to vouch, or your message is just noise.
cards.truth:
A referral carries risk for the referrer, which is exactly why it works.
• The bridge person spends their own reputation when they introduce you.
• Your target reads the intro as pre-screened, not random.
• Most people ask for the intro wrong — vague, open-ended, easy to ignore.
cards.remember: A stranger vouching for you is worth ten of your own words.
cards.theySee: A trusted name saying 'you two should talk,' with a clear reason attached.

signals.t: LinkedIn or a colleague shows a real, active mutual connection.
The mutual has agreed in words to make the introduction.
You gave the mutual one clear line explaining why the intro matters.

steps.title: Write the intro for them
steps.desc: Draft the two-line email so the mutual can forward it unchanged.

steps.title: Give one clean reason
steps.desc: State exactly why this specific intro matters, not a vague 'connect us'.

steps.title: Follow up with the mutual, not the target
steps.desc: Check in with the mutual after 5 days if nothing moved yet.

cards.script: "Would you be open to introducing me to [Name]? I'm looking to ask about X — happy to draft the intro so it's a 10-second forward for you."
cards.watchFor: The mutual forwards your exact draft within a few days, unedited.
cards.ifItFails: The mutual agrees but never sends it — good intentions, no urgency on their end. Don't nag; give them a deadline tied to something real. Send: "No rush, but I'm reaching out to a few people on this by Friday — happy to go direct if easier for you."
cards.counter:
If someone hands you a ready-made intro to forward, notice you're the one taking the risk.
• Check the draft is accurate before you send your name on it.
• Edit it in your own voice so it's clearly your endorsement.
• Say no if you don't actually know enough to vouch.
cards.insight: An introduction is a loan of reputation, and loans get called in eventually. The next question is what you do with the meeting the loan bought you — a wasted intro burns the bridge for good.
cards.when: You have a mutual connection to your target but haven't asked for the introduction yet.
cards.example: Marcus asked a mutual friend to forward a two-line note to a division head, drafting it himself so it took the friend ten seconds. The division head replied to the forwarded note the same afternoon.

cards.title: Lead With Their Problem, Not Your Ask
cards.hook: Nobody reads past line one to find your ask. Line one has to be about them.
cards.truth:
Busy people scan the first sentence and decide to keep reading or delete.
• A message that opens with their problem earns one more sentence of attention.
• A message that opens with your ask gets deleted before line two.
• Most people lead with 'I' and lose the reader instantly.
cards.remember: Open with their problem — save your ask for line three.
cards.theySee: A message that names their exact problem before asking for anything.

signals.t: Your first sentence names their problem, not your background.
Your specific ask sits in line three or later, not line one.
You attach a real number to the problem you're naming.

steps.title: Name their problem in line one
steps.desc: Write one sentence about their exact challenge, using their own words.

steps.title: Prove you can help in line two
steps.desc: State one concrete result you got on the same problem.

steps.title: Ask in line three, small
steps.desc: Make the ask one sentence, and make it easy to say yes to.

cards.script: "Saw your Q2 churn number is up — I fixed the same issue at [Company] and cut it 18% in six weeks. Worth a 10-minute call?"
cards.watchFor: They reply with a question about the result, not about who you are.
cards.ifItFails: They reply 'not a priority right now' — meaning the problem you named isn't the one keeping them up at night. Ask one direct question to find the real one, don't re-pitch the same angle. Send: "Got it — what is the top priority instead? Might still be useful there."
cards.counter:
If a stranger opens by naming your exact problem, check if the fix is real or just a pitch.
• Ask for one specific proof point before believing the number.
• Notice if the ask that follows is small or a foot in the door.
• Answer only the size of ask you're actually ready to give.
cards.insight: Self-interest is the only language that gets read past line one. The next problem is proof — a claim with no number attached reads the same as flattery.
cards.when: You're writing the first cold message to someone far above you.
cards.example: Sofia wrote to a VP naming the exact churn number from his last earnings call before asking anything. He replied asking how she knew, then asked for a call.

cards.title: Keep the First Message Under 60 Words
cards.hook: Every extra sentence is a chance to lose them. Cut until it hurts, then cut once more.
cards.truth:
Senior people read on a phone between meetings, in stolen seconds.
• A message under 60 words gets read in full, every time.
• A message over 150 words gets skimmed or skipped entirely.
• Most people add context nobody asked for and bury the actual ask.
cards.remember: If it doesn't fit on one phone screen, they won't finish it.
cards.theySee: A message they can read and answer between two meetings, not homework.

signals.t: The whole message fits without scrolling on a phone.
Your message skips your resume and history entirely.
The message asks exactly one thing, not two or three.

steps.title: Write the long version first
steps.desc: Get every thought out in a rough draft, no editing yet.

steps.title: Cut every sentence that isn't the problem, proof, or ask
steps.desc: Delete backstory, pleasantries, and context sentences.

steps.title: Read it out loud once
steps.desc: If it takes more than 20 seconds to say, cut again.

cards.script: "Quick one: your team's onboarding drop-off matches a problem I solved last year, cut it 30%. Worth 10 minutes?"
cards.watchFor: They reply within the same day, matching your message's short length.
cards.ifItFails: The short version gets no reply either — length wasn't the actual issue, relevance was. Rewrite around a sharper, more specific problem instead of trimming the same generic one further. Send a completely different angle, still under 60 words, testing a new problem.
cards.counter:
If a short, sharp message lands in your inbox, judge it on the ask, not the polish.
• A tight message can still be a bad or oversized ask.
• Ask one clarifying question before committing any time.
• Answer with an equally short reply — match their format.
cards.insight: Brevity signals respect for someone's time better than any compliment can. The next problem is that short is easy to write badly — cutting words without cutting the wrong idea is the real skill.
cards.when: You've drafted your first message and it's longer than a few sentences.
cards.example: Dmitri cut his message from 220 words to 41 before sending it to a division president. The president answered on his phone between meetings, same day.

cards.title: Give Them an Easy Yes in the First Line
cards.hook: Don't ask for a meeting. Ask for a one-word answer first.
cards.truth:
A big ask forces a real decision. A tiny ask feels free to grant.
• A yes-or-no question gets answered faster than an open-ended one.
• Once they say yes to something small, saying yes again feels natural.
• Most people ask for 30 minutes right away and get ignored.
cards.remember: Make the first yes tiny — small yeses are easy to give.
cards.theySee: A question that takes five seconds to answer, not a calendar decision.

signals.t: Your ask can be answered with one word.
The first ask doesn't mention minutes, calls, or meetings yet.
You have a bigger ask ready for after the first yes.

steps.title: Turn your real ask into a yes/no
steps.desc: Rewrite 'can we meet' as 'is this worth a look, yes or no.'

steps.title: Send only that question first
steps.desc: Leave the meeting request out of the first message entirely.

steps.title: Follow the yes with the real ask fast
steps.desc: Send the calendar link within the hour of their yes.

cards.script: "Quick one before I take more of your time — is a 30% drop in onboarding cost still a live problem for your team? Yes or no is fine."
cards.watchFor: They answer with just 'yes' or a short confirmation, no hedging.
cards.ifItFails: They answer 'depends' instead of yes or no — the question wasn't sharp enough to force a binary answer. Narrow it further into something that truly only has two answers. Send: "Fair — simpler version: worth 10 minutes this week, yes or no?"
cards.counter:
If someone asks you a tiny yes/no question first, notice the ladder being built.
• A yes to something small is being used to justify a yes to something bigger.
• Answer the small question honestly, without assuming you owe the next step.
• Decide the bigger ask fresh, on its own terms.
cards.insight: Small commitments create their own gravity — people keep saying yes to stay consistent with themselves. The next problem is timing the jump from small yes to real ask before the moment cools off.
cards.when: You're about to send a first message that asks for a meeting or a call.
cards.example: Aisha asked a hiring VP just one yes-or-no question about a hiring problem before asking for a call. The VP wrote back 'yes' in nine minutes, and Aisha sent the calendar link within the hour.

cards.title: Never Ask for '15 Minutes of Your Time'
cards.hook: Time asks get ignored. Value asks get answered. Nobody wants to give away minutes for nothing back.
cards.truth:
'15 minutes' names a cost with no promised reward, so the brain defaults to no.
• People protect their calendar reflexively against any minute request.
• A stated result reframes the same ask as a trade, not a gift.
• Most people think politeness excuses a vague ask. It doesn't.
cards.remember: Say what they get, not how many minutes it costs them.
cards.theySee: A specific trade — what they get for the time, not an open-ended favor.

signals.t: Your message never states a number of minutes.
You state exactly what they walk away with.
The ask reads as an exchange, not a one-way favor.

steps.title: Delete every mention of minutes
steps.desc: Remove '15 minutes,' '30 minutes,' or any time reference.

steps.title: Name the result instead
steps.desc: State the exact thing they get: a number, a fix, a contact.

steps.title: Let them set the length
steps.desc: Say 'however long makes sense for you' instead of naming a duration.

cards.script: "I can walk you through the exact fix that cut our churn 18% — whatever length makes sense on your end."
cards.watchFor: They propose the meeting length themselves, unprompted.
cards.ifItFails: They still decline, saying they're too busy — the result wasn't compelling enough to beat a full calendar. Shrink the ask to something with zero calendar cost: a two-line written answer instead of a meeting. Send: "No problem — even a two-line reply on what you'd want to see would help."
cards.counter:
If someone offers a result instead of asking for your minutes, check if the result is real.
• Ask for one proof point before agreeing to any length of call.
• Notice if 'however long you want' is really a foot in the door.
• Set the length yourself and hold to it.
cards.insight: People don't guard their time — they guard against wasting it on nothing. The next problem is delivering on the promised result once they actually show up.
cards.when: You're about to write 'can I get 15 minutes of your time' in a message.
cards.example: Leo dropped '15 minutes' from his message entirely and just named the exact number he could save the exec's team. The exec proposed the call length himself instead of Leo asking.

cards.title: Reply Inside the Hour They Answer
cards.hook: They replied because right now, for one hour, you mattered. Don't waste that window sleeping on it.
cards.truth:
Attention from someone senior doesn't sit and wait for you.
• Their reply means you're on their mind for a short window now.
• A slow reply back reads as low priority, even if you're just busy.
• Most people treat any reply as safe and answer whenever it's convenient.
cards.remember: Answer fast — their interest cools by the hour, not the day.
cards.theySee: Someone who was clearly waiting and ready, not scrambling to catch up.

signals.t: You have alerts on for their name specifically.
Your response goes out within 60 minutes of theirs.
You already have your next message drafted before they even reply.

steps.title: Draft your next message before they reply
steps.desc: Write the follow-up now, before you know if or when they'll answer.

steps.title: Set an alert for their name
steps.desc: Turn on notifications for their email or platform so you see it fast.

steps.title: Answer within the hour, every time
steps.desc: Reply inside 60 minutes even if the answer is short.

cards.script: "Great, thanks for the fast reply — does Thursday at 2pm or Friday at 10am work better on your end?"
cards.watchFor: They confirm a time within the same conversation thread, same day.
cards.ifItFails: You reply fast but then hear nothing for days — they got pulled into something else and you're now competing with their whole inbox again. Send one more nudge after 3 days, short, with a new fact attached so it doesn't read as a bare bump. "Following up — also just saw X happened, which makes this more time-sensitive."
cards.counter:
If someone replies to you within minutes every single time, notice what that costs them.
• Fast replies can mean eagerness or can mean desperation — read the content, not the speed.
• Don't reward speed alone with more of your time.
• Judge each message on its content, every time.
cards.insight: Momentum is the real currency in any exchange with someone busier than you. The next problem is that speed without substance just gets you a faster no.
cards.when: Someone far above you finally replies to your message.
cards.example: When a division head replied to Rina at 4:47pm on a Friday, she answered by 5:10pm with two meeting times ready. They were on a call by Tuesday.

cards.title: Bring Something New to the Meeting, Not a Recap
cards.hook: They already read your pitch. Repeating it in the meeting wastes the meeting.
cards.truth:
A senior person already decided the meeting was worth it — the pitch already worked.
• Repeating your written pitch out loud adds nothing and bores them.
• One new fact, number, or option earns the second meeting.
• Most people show up and recap what they already sent.
cards.remember: Don't repeat yourself — bring one new thing they haven't seen.
cards.theySee: Someone who kept working the problem since the last message, not someone who coasted.

signals.t: You bring one number or fact not in your original message.
Your opening skips restating the original pitch.
Your ask in the meeting is more specific than the one in writing.

steps.title: Find one new thing since your message
steps.desc: Research, test, or ask a contact for one fact from the last few days.

steps.title: Cut the recap from your opening
steps.desc: Skip restating your pitch; assume they remember why they said yes.

steps.title: Open with the new thing
steps.desc: Start the meeting with what changed since you last wrote.

cards.script: "Since we last talked, I actually tested this with a smaller team — here's what happened."
cards.watchFor: They lean in or start taking notes at the new information, not before.
cards.ifItFails: They seem distracted even through the new information — the meeting itself might be the wrong format for what you're pitching. Offer to send a one-page follow-up instead of pushing harder live. Say: "Sounds like this might work better in writing — mind if I send a short follow-up you can read on your own time?"
cards.counter:
If someone opens a meeting with brand-new information you didn't expect, notice the shift in leverage.
• They're resetting the terms of the conversation on their information, not yours.
• Ask one clarifying question before reacting to the new fact.
• Don't let a surprise fact rush you into agreeing to something bigger.
cards.insight: Repetition reads as laziness to someone who already said yes once. The next problem is finding new material fast enough between message and meeting to actually earn a second one.
cards.when: You've landed the meeting and you're preparing what to bring.
cards.example: Before his second meeting with a regional president, Carlos ran one small pilot test overnight and opened with the result instead of repeating his deck. The president leaned forward and asked for the full plan on the spot.

cards.title: Let Them Talk First
cards.hook: Whoever talks first gives up the most information. Ask, then wait.
cards.truth:
In any status gap, the higher-status person expects to lead the room.
• Asking them an open question first flatters that expectation.
• What they say first tells you exactly what to pitch back.
• Most people fill the silence with their own pitch instead of listening.
cards.remember: Ask one open question, then stay quiet and let them talk.
cards.theySee: Someone who respects their time enough to ask instead of perform.

signals.t: Your first sentence in the meeting is a question, not a statement.
You let a pause sit for 3+ seconds after asking.
You visibly write down what they say in the first two minutes.

steps.title: Open with one real question
steps.desc: Ask what's actually on their mind about the topic right now.

steps.title: Wait through the silence
steps.desc: Count to five in your head before saying anything else.

steps.title: Pitch back their own words
steps.desc: Shape your ask around exactly what they just told you.

cards.script: "Before I get into what I brought — what's the actual state of this on your end right now?"
cards.watchFor: They talk for over a minute without you interrupting once.
cards.ifItFails: They deflect with 'you go first' — some senior people are trained to keep information close. Don't force it; give a short version of your point, then loop back to your question. Say: "Sure — quick version is X. Now, back to you: what's the real bottleneck on your side?"
cards.counter:
If someone opens a meeting by asking you an open question, notice you're giving up information for free.
• Answer in general terms before revealing your specific numbers.
• Ask your own question back before going deeper.
• Match how much they've shared before you share more.
cards.insight: Whoever asks the questions runs the meeting, not whoever talks the most. The next problem is using what they told you without sounding like you're reading it back verbatim.
cards.when: The meeting has just started and you're tempted to launch into your pitch.
cards.example: In her first meeting with a company's COO, Yuki asked one open question and then said nothing for ten full seconds. The COO talked for six minutes, handing her exactly what she needed to pitch back.

cards.title: End the Meeting Before They Want To
cards.hook: The best meetings end five minutes early. Leaving first is a power move, not rudeness.
cards.truth:
Whoever ends the meeting controls the last impression.
• Ending early signals you have other places to be, which raises your value.
• They leave with unanswered curiosity instead of talked-out fatigue.
• Most people ramble to fill the whole scheduled time and dilute the win.
cards.remember: Stop early — leave them wanting the next conversation, not the door.
cards.theySee: Someone with a full schedule, not someone with nothing else to do.

signals.t: You mention the time and offer to wrap up first.
You leave one question or topic clearly unfinished on purpose.
You propose the specific next step before they ask for one.

steps.title: Watch for the peak
steps.desc: Notice the moment energy is highest, usually mid-conversation, not the end.

steps.title: Name the time and offer to stop
steps.desc: Say you know they're busy and offer to wrap up early.

steps.title: Propose the next step yourself
steps.desc: Suggest the follow-up action before they have to ask for one.

cards.script: "I know you've got a hard stop — let's leave it here, and I'll send over the one thing we didn't get to."
cards.watchFor: They ask to extend the meeting or schedule the next one on the spot.
cards.ifItFails: They take the early exit at face value and the conversation just ends, no next step offered. Don't wait for them to reach back out — send the follow-up within the hour with the open thread attached. Send: "Here's the piece we didn't get to — want to grab 10 more minutes this week?"
cards.counter:
If someone cuts a good meeting short on purpose, notice the tactic.
• Don't chase them for more time right then — it reads as needy.
• Wait for their promised follow-up before reacting.
• If it doesn't arrive in a few days, reach out once, plainly.
cards.insight: Scarcity works on attention the same way it works on anything people want more of. Do not use this on someone who reads an early exit as disrespect — a formal, protocol-driven executive expects the full scheduled time. The next problem is having a genuinely good open thread to leave behind, since a fake one gets noticed.
cards.when: The meeting is going well and you're tempted to keep it going.
cards.example: Ben ended a strong meeting with a division head five minutes early, on purpose, leaving one topic open. The division head emailed that night asking to finish the conversation.

cards.title: Ask for the Smallest Favor First
cards.hook: Don't ask for the job. Ask for one intro, one look, one name.
cards.truth:
A person who says yes to something small starts seeing themselves as your ally.
• The size of the first favor sets the ceiling for what feels reasonable next.
• A tiny favor costs them almost nothing but commits them to you.
• Most people ask for the big favor first and get a polite no.
cards.principle: Cialdini: Commitment and Consistency — Foot in the Door
cards.remember: Ask for something tiny first — big favors get easier after that.
cards.theySee: A request so small it feels rude to refuse.

signals.t: The favor takes them under 5 minutes to grant.
You ask for one specific name, intro, or piece of feedback.
You already know the bigger ask you'll make after this one.

steps.title: Pick the smallest useful favor
steps.desc: Choose one intro, one document, or one opinion, nothing bigger.

steps.title: Make it a two-minute ask
steps.desc: Word it so granting it takes them under two minutes.

steps.title: Wait before asking for more
steps.desc: Let the small favor land fully before naming the next one.

cards.script: "One small ask — could you point me to whoever runs vendor selection on your team? That's all I need for now."
cards.watchFor: They grant the small favor within a day, without asking why.
cards.ifItFails: They ignore even the tiny ask — attention has already cooled past the point a small favor can revive. Don't escalate the size of the ask to compensate; go back to bridge-building instead, one useful update at a time. Send one piece of value with no ask attached and restart the ladder slower.
cards.counter:
If someone asks you for something suspiciously small, notice the ladder forming.
• A tiny favor is often a test for a bigger one to come.
• Grant it if it truly costs you nothing, and track that you did.
• Set the size of the next ask yourself, don't let them escalate it.
cards.insight: Foot-in-the-door works because refusing small things feels petty. The next problem is climbing the ladder without a rung breaking — ask too big too soon and the whole thing collapses.
cards.when: You finally have their attention and want to turn it into something real.
cards.example: Instead of asking a hiring exec for a job, Kwame asked for one name: whoever ran vendor reviews. The small ask got granted in a day, and it became the opening that led to the actual role three weeks later.

cards.title: Turn the Favor Into a Story They Can Tell
cards.hook: People don't help you. They help the story where they're the one who spotted talent early.
cards.truth:
A favor that makes the giver look sharp gets granted faster than one that just helps you.
• People love being the person who discovered someone before they were known.
• Give them a story with a good ending, and they tell it for free.
• Most people ask for help without giving the helper anything to say later.
cards.principle: Greene: Law 13 — Self-Interest as Social Currency
cards.remember: Make helping you a good story they can tell later.
cards.theySee: A chance to be the mentor in a story with a visible future payoff.

signals.t: Your ask has a clear before-and-after they'd enjoy describing.
You explicitly note they'd be first to back this.
There's a real chance the outcome becomes publicly visible later.

steps.title: Frame the ask as a bet on you
steps.desc: Say what you're trying to become, not just what you need now.

steps.title: Name the story they'd be telling
steps.desc: Say out loud what they get to say later: 'I backed this early.'

steps.title: Follow up when the story pays off
steps.desc: Tell them the result later so the story actually completes.

cards.script: "If this works, you'll be the person who took a chance on it early — that's the ask."
cards.watchFor: They mention you or the favor to someone else, unprompted, later.
cards.ifItFails: They grant the favor but never mention it again — the story framing didn't land, or they don't see themselves as a mentor type. Drop the story angle for that person permanently and switch to a pure self-interest frame for any future ask. Send: "Appreciated the help — separately, here's a number that might matter for your own numbers."
cards.counter:
If someone frames your help as a story you get to tell, notice the flattery.
• Ask what you actually get besides the story, before agreeing.
• Grant only what costs you little regardless of the story's appeal.
• Follow up in six months to see if the story was even true.
cards.insight: Ego is a renewable resource people spend on you gladly if you let them keep the good line for themselves. The next problem is delivering a real result — a story with a bad ending gets told too, just not by them.
cards.when: You're asking a senior person for a favor and want to raise the odds of a yes.
cards.example: Instead of just asking for advice, Sana told an investor she was trying to become the person who fixed churn industry-wide, and the investor got to be the one who spotted it early. He introduced her at a conference himself, unprompted, months later.

cards.title: Give Them Credit Before They Ask
cards.hook: The fastest way to get a second favor is to make the first one look good on them, publicly, first. Don't wait to be asked for credit.
cards.truth:
People remember who made them look good more than who they helped.
• Public credit costs you nothing and buys their loyalty for the next ask.
• It proves you're safe to help again without loss of status.
• Most people take the favor and stay quiet, wasting the easiest follow-up move.
cards.principle: Greene: Law 1 — Never Outshine the Master, Applied Upward
cards.remember: Say their name in the win before anyone asks who helped.
cards.theySee: Their name attached to a visible win, without having to ask for it.

signals.t: You name them in a post, email thread, or update, unprompted.
You name the exact thing they did, not a vague thanks.
You give the credit within days of the result landing.

steps.title: Wait for a real result
steps.desc: Don't give credit for advice until it actually produces something.

steps.title: Name them specifically, in public
steps.desc: Post or email naming exactly what they did and what happened.

steps.title: Send them the credit directly too
steps.desc: Also send them a private note, not just the public one.

cards.script: "Wanted to flag — [Name]'s intro led directly to this deal closing. Grateful for the push."
cards.watchFor: They react to the public credit and reference it again themselves later.
cards.ifItFails: They seem uncomfortable with public credit — some senior people prefer to stay invisible in other people's wins. Switch to private-only credit for that person going forward, delivered directly and specifically. Send: "Didn't want to make it public since I know you prefer that, but wanted you to know directly — this worked because of your intro."
cards.counter:
If someone credits you publicly right after you helped them, notice the timing.
• Public credit can be genuine gratitude or a calculated move for your loyalty.
• Accept it plainly, don't over-thank them back into an obligation.
• Judge their next ask on its own terms, not on the warm glow.
cards.insight: Credit is the cheapest currency that exists and almost nobody spends it on purpose. The next problem is consistency — one grateful post means little if you vanish after that.
cards.when: Someone senior gave you a favor, intro, or piece of advice that worked.
cards.example: After a VP's intro led to a signed deal, Owen posted publicly naming the VP and the exact intro that made it happen. The VP referenced that post himself in a meeting three months later.

cards.title: Send the Second Message From a Different Angle
cards.hook: The same message twice just proves you have nothing new to say. Change the angle, not the volume.
cards.truth:
Silence after one message usually means the angle missed, not the timing.
• A second identical message reads as pressure, not persistence.
• A new angle tests a completely different reason they might care.
• Most people just bump the same message and get the same silence.
cards.remember: Don't repeat yourself — try a completely different reason to write.
cards.theySee: A completely different reason to respond, not a nag about the first one.

signals.t: Your second message names a different problem or fact entirely.
At least 5-7 days passed since the first message.
The message doesn't mention 'following up' or 'just checking in.'

steps.title: Wait a real week
steps.desc: Let 5-7 days pass before sending anything else.

steps.title: Find a second, different reason
steps.desc: Pick a fact, event, or angle you didn't use the first time.

steps.title: Write it as a fresh message
steps.desc: Don't reference the first message at all, just start clean.

cards.script: "Different note — saw your team just hit X. Given that, thought this might land differently: [new angle]."
cards.watchFor: They reply engaging with the new angle specifically, not a generic apology for missing the first.
cards.ifItFails: The second angle also gets silence — two misses means the target or the channel is wrong, not the wording. Switch channels entirely, email to a platform DM or the reverse, or move to the introduction route instead of a third direct attempt. Ask a bridge contact for a two-line intro rather than sending a third cold message.
cards.counter:
If a second message arrives with a totally different angle than the first, notice the persistence.
• They're testing which reason gets through to you.
• Answer honestly on whichever angle you actually care about, if any.
• If neither interests you, say so once, clearly, to stop the cycle.
cards.insight: Silence is information about the angle, not about you as a person. The next problem is knowing how many angles are worth trying before it's time to stop.
cards.when: You sent a first message a week or more ago and heard nothing back.
cards.example: After a week of silence, Talia sent a second message to a division president with a totally different angle — a competitor's new move instead of her original pitch. He replied within a day, engaging directly with the new angle.

cards.title: Go Around Through Someone They Manage
cards.hook: The top person delegates almost everything. Their team can say yes without them ever seeing your name.
cards.truth:
Most requests to senior people get delegated down before they're even read fully.
• Someone on their team likely already handles requests exactly like yours.
• Going straight to that person skips the queue entirely.
• Most people keep emailing the top of the chain and never route down.
cards.remember: Ask the person who reports to them — delegated answers still count.
cards.theySee: A request routed correctly to the person who actually owns it.

signals.t: You can see who reports to your target on LinkedIn or the company site.
Public posts show someone else handling this type of request.
The same name appears as 'reply to' or contact on related public items.

steps.title: Find their direct reports
steps.desc: Check the org chart, company site, or LinkedIn for who reports to them.

steps.title: Identify who owns your topic
steps.desc: Pick the report whose role matches your specific ask.

steps.title: Message that person directly
steps.desc: Send your pitch to them, mentioning you'd first tried the top.

cards.script: "I reached out to [Name] directly on this — realized it's probably more your area. Same question: [ask]."
cards.watchFor: The report answers substantively and offers to loop in their boss if needed.
cards.ifItFails: The report also goes quiet — the whole team may be triaging you as low priority based on how the ask reads, not who received it. Rewrite the ask sharper and smaller before trying a third contact on the team. Send a version with a number and a one-line yes/no question, to a third name on the team.
cards.counter:
If someone routes around your boss straight to you, notice what that means.
• They likely already tried the top and got nothing.
• Decide if this is actually your area before engaging.
• Loop your boss in briefly if the topic matters, so no surprise later.
cards.insight: Organizations delegate by design, which means the top person's silence rarely means no. The next problem is picking the right report — the wrong one just adds a second silence to the pile.
cards.when: You've messaged the top person directly with no response for weeks.
cards.example: After three weeks of silence from a CFO, Dev found the CFO's direct report who handled vendor onboarding and pitched her instead. She answered within a day and looped the CFO in only once it mattered.

cards.title: Know When to Let the Silence Be the Answer
cards.hook: Chasing a ghost costs you time and your reputation with everyone watching. Know the number where you stop.
cards.truth:
Silence after three genuine attempts, on different angles and channels, is a decision.
• Continuing past that point reads as desperation, not persistence.
• The time spent chasing one no-reply could open two new doors instead.
• Most people can't tell the difference between patience and wasting their own time.
cards.remember: Three failed tries means no — stop chasing and move on.
cards.theySee: Nothing — they never notice the fourth message because they already filtered you out.

signals.t: You've tried three distinct angles or contacts with zero response.
Each attempt got less engagement than the one before it.
More than a month has passed since your first message.

steps.title: Count your real attempts
steps.desc: Write down each distinct attempt, angle, and channel you've used.

steps.title: Set your own stop number
steps.desc: Decide in advance, three tries or four, before you're emotionally invested.

steps.title: Redirect the time you'd spend chasing
steps.desc: Put your next hour into a brand-new target instead.

cards.script: "Not chasing this further, but the offer stands anytime — reach out whenever it's useful."
cards.watchFor: Months later, they reply out of nowhere — proof the silence was timing, not a verdict.
cards.ifItFails: You stop, but you're wrong and they actually would have said yes with one more try — this happens, and there's no way to know for certain. Leave one clean, permanent door open instead of vanishing completely, a single evergreen line they can act on anytime. Send a closing message with that line and nothing else attached.
cards.counter:
If someone announces they're done chasing you, notice the door they leave open.
• A graceful stop is often a final test of whether you care enough to respond.
• If the offer is genuinely useful, respond even after the stated stop.
• Don't assume silence from you means the value disappeared too.
cards.insight: Knowing when to stop is the harder skill than knowing how to start — most people either quit at message one or chase forever. The next question is whether you spend the saved time on a new target or on nothing at all.
cards.when: You've tried the target, a new angle, and their team, and heard nothing across all three.
cards.example: After three tries and three angles with total silence from a media exec, Farah stopped and moved her energy to a new target that week. Eight months later, the exec resurfaced out of nowhere, ready to talk.
